newsitem.title: UK: Second Falkland oil licence round may be delayed.
newsitem.headline: Second Falkland oil licence round may be delayed.

text.p: The second round of Falkland Islands offshore oil exploration licensing may suffer bureaucratic delays at the hands of an Anglo-Argentine commission, the former oil licensing administrator for the islands' government said on Wednesday.
But oil company interest in the first licensing round was unexpectedly high, particularly in the shallower northern blocks, John Martin added.
"The response was far better than we anticipated, but all the bids were in the north," Martin told a conference.
Unlike the first round, which was in exclusively Falkland Islands waters, the second round is governed by an Anglo-Argentine commission which has met only twice in the past 12 months.
"The joint commission is turning into a word shop," Martin said.
"They have got to marry two taxes, two sets of environmental regulations, two sets of operational regulations...and I don't know when it will be issued.
"They talk about within the next two years, but I think that's very optimistic because it's only now that they've agreed an agenda of what to talk about."

Martin said he was surprised by the level of interest in the first licensing round, given the problem of moving seismic equipment and drilling rigs out to this remote area and the cost of building up a service infrastructure on the Falklands Islands.
"Then of course there was the political overhang, which certainly turned away a lot of American companies," he added.
First round licences, awarded last month, were won by consortia led by Amerada Hess, Royal Dutch/Shell, LASMO Plc, International Petroleum Corp and local firm Desire Petroleum.

"To my certain knowledge, all the operators got phone calls from the American companies who hadn't come in to say, 'Is there room in your group?'... But it was too bad because none of these companies gave any equity to anybody. They just want to wait and see what they've got," Martin said.
He said it was still not known whether any commercial oil discoveries would be made around the Falklands, but the sedimentary rock formations were of the same age as those in the North Sea.
"It is one of the few areas of the world where the oil industry has not yet drilled. It's absolutely unknown," he added.
